(Monday night through Saturday)
Issued at 109 AM MDT Sun Sep 27 2026

Tuesday morning begins the peak event period for widespread and 
persistent shower and thunderstorm activity across all of NM. The 
combination of daily record level PWAT moisture reaching 1.30" at 
ABQ from the insurgent remnants of Hurricane Polo and the favorable 
dynamic forcing aloft ahead of the H5 low over western AZ will just 
about maximize the rainfall production potential for this event. 
Multiple waves of showers and storms capable of produce heavy 
rainfall will stream SW-NE across the state. And while showers and 
storms look to expand and break out across the eastern plains of NM 
by Monday night and Tuesday morning, the brunt of Hurricane Polo's 
remnants crossing the southeastern half of NM doesn't look to arrive 
until Tuesday afternoon or evening. There is some uncertainty still 
regarding the timing of that specific part of this event. Given the 
delay for the onset of precipitation and period of most intense 
rainfall, a second segment of the Flash Flood Watch for areas along 
and east of the central mountain chain starts Monday evening, with 
all areas of the Watch lasting at least until Wednesday morning. 

Much of the northern half of NM will likely see the Flash Flood 
Watch extended longer into Wednesday as a dry slot punches in behind 
the exiting remnants of Hurricane Polo by this time. The H5 low 
becomes the main player thereafter, centered somewhere over west-
central to central NM to start the day. Wrap around moisture, likely 
forming a TROWAL feature across northeastern NM into southeastern CO 
will keep showers with embedded storms lasting thru the day 
Wednesday over these areas. Drier northwesterly flow fills in behind 
the H5 low as it exits eastward over the TX/OK Panhandles and/or 
western KS sometime Wednesday evening to Thursday morning. As such, 
precipitation looks to exit northeastern NM last, perhaps as late as 
Friday morning. 

Uncertainty regarding the overall duration of this event and when
rain will end is still relatively high given the complex 
atmospheric dynamics of the remnants of Hurricane Polo being 
absorbed into the circulation of the H5 low, or if it gets swung 
out and ejected out over the Great Plains. Therefore, the 
residence time of this event over NM still has a range of around 
24-hours different between the shortest and longest times. 

All told, 24-hr rainfall amounts look to range 1-2 inches each day, 
with higher amounts upwards of 2-3 inches Tuesday thru Wednesday 
morning over eastern NM. Event total rainfall amounts look to favor 
the 2-3 inch range for the western half of the state, and 3-4 inch 
range over the eastern plains. Locally higher amounts upwards of 4-6 
inches cannot be ruled out over portions of eastern NM, or within 
mountainous areas where orographics will play an additional factor 
squeezing more moisture out of the atmosphere. 

While conditions clear out Friday into next weekend. Impacts are 
likely to remain across the forecast area in the form of river 
flooding. The coverage and amount of rain forecast will take time 
work its way through drainage basins and river systems. Rises at 
specific locations along rivers may take hours to days after rain 
has ended to occur. Be vigilant and do not be caught off guard even 
as the skies clear. 

We've had hurricane remnants surge over NM before with less flash 
flood risk, why is this event different? Many events of hurricane 
remnants moving over NM in recent years have been on their own and 
not accompanied with another nearby storm system that was capable of 
metaphorically squeezing more rain out of it. Therefore, they were 
mostly light to moderate rain intensities and/or overcast cloud 
cover with more isolated bouts of heavy rain. This event has that 
accompanying storm system swinging through from CA, squeezing more 
moisture out of the remnants of Hurricane Polo. The other factor, is 
the abundant rainfall New Mexico has seen these past two weeks. This 
has led to near-record to record level soil moisture inundation over 
most of the state for late September. This means, the ground has 
little to no more room to absorb rainfall before runoff begins. All 
told, these multiple factors are all adding up in the wrong 
direction to bring a heightened flash flood risk over the state. Be 
weather aware, be vigilant, have multiple ways of receiving warnings 
during this time.
